specPoints.text: know and use the relationship between power, current and voltage: power = current × voltage
and apply the relationship to the selection of appropriate fuses

primer.text: Every mains appliance carries a power rating, and that rating governs both the current it draws and the fuse that guards it. This note builds the relationship between power, current and voltage, shows the formula-triangle shortcut for rearranging it, and then applies the same equation to choosing a safe fuse size from the standard ratings.

lessons.title: Electrical power
lessons.opening: Power measures how fast a device moves energy: the more joules it transfers each second, the more powerful it is. For an electrical device the power rises with both the voltage across it and the current through it. This lesson assembles the equation P = I × V, fixes the watt as a joule per second, and shows how the formula triangle hands you the two rearrangements.
keyPoints: Power is the rate of energy transfer — the amount of energy a device moves each second.
A device's power grows with both the voltage across it and the current through it.
The equation of record is P = I × V, with power in watts, current in amperes and voltage in volts.
One watt means one joule of energy transferred per second.
A formula triangle gives the rearrangements V = P ÷ I and I = P ÷ V without any algebra.

low.restatement: Power is how quickly energy is moved; the equation P = I × V ties it to the current and the voltage.
low.analogy: Think of a water wheel: the more water per second (current) and the bigger the drop (voltage), the faster it grinds.
low.examPointer: Always write the unit of every quantity when substituting — W, A and V keep the answer in watts.

medium.restatement: The watt is a derived unit: one joule per second, so the per-second view of power is built into the equation itself.
medium.analogy: A payslip: the voltage is the hourly rate, the current is the hours worked, and the power is the money earned per day.
medium.examPointer: The formula triangle hides the correct product or quotient — cover the unknown and read off the relationship.

check.stem: Power is defined as the rate of:

options.explanation: Charge flow per second would be current, not power.
Power counts the energy moved in every second of operation.
Voltage is not counted over time; this mixes the two ideas.
That inverts the relationship between energy and current.

check.stem: One watt is the same as:

options.explanation: That defines a volt.
That defines an ampere.
Neither quantity appears in the power relationship.
The watt is exactly one joule of energy moved every second.

check.stem: A 4 A motor runs at 48 W. The potential difference across it is:

options.explanation: That multiplies instead of dividing: 48 × 4 is meaningless here.
That divides the current by the power — the wrong way round.
Adding the two quantities carries no physical meaning.

check.stem: In the equation P = I × V, the quantity I stands for:

options.explanation: I is the symbol for current in this relationship.
Insulation is a safety feature, not part of this equation.
Intensity does not enter this equation.
Ohms belong to resistance, a different relationship.

check.stem: Doubling both the current through and the voltage across a device multiplies its power by:

options.text: two, because only one factor counts
options.explanation: Both factors enter the product, so both changes count.
P = I × V, and 2 × 2 multiplies the power by four.

options.text: no change, because the effects cancel
options.explanation: The two changes reinforce rather than cancel.
Only two quantities multiply in P = I × V.

check.stem: State the equation linking power, current and voltage, naming the unit of each quantity.
check.modelAnswer: P = I × V, with power in watts, current in amperes and voltage in volts.

check.stem: What does one watt equal in energy terms?
check.modelAnswer: One watt is one joule of energy transferred every second.

check.stem: Explain why the formula triangle is a dependable way to rearrange P = I × V.
check.modelAnswer: Covering the quantity you want leaves the other two touching, which gives the exact product or quotient — V = P ÷ I or I = P ÷ V — so no algebra step can go wrong.

check.stem: An oven draws 10 A from a 230 V supply. Calculate its power.

lessons.title: Selecting fuses
lessons.opening: A fuse is the sacrificial guard in an appliance: a thin wire that melts when the current outruns the safe value, breaking the circuit before damage spreads. Choosing one is a two-step habit — compute the current the appliance needs, then step one size up from the standard ratings.
keyPoints: A fuse protects an appliance by melting its thin wire when the current grows too large.
Melting breaks the circuit, so the surge cannot damage the equipment or start a fire.
Household fuses come in standard ratings of 3 A, 5 A and 13 A.
The current an appliance needs is found from I = P ÷ V using its power and the mains voltage.
Always fit the next size up: a rating too low blows needlessly, one too high reacts too late.

low.restatement: A fuse melts when the current is too big, which breaks the circuit and stops the damage.
low.analogy: Like a sacrificial link in a chain — it snaps first so the rest of the chain survives.
low.examPointer: Fuse questions want two steps: find the current, then pick the next standard rating up.

medium.restatement: The melting point of the wire is calibrated by its rating, so the fuse tolerates the working current but not a fault surge.
medium.analogy: A nightclub doorman with a strict cap: a slightly larger crowd than usual gets in, a surge does not.
medium.examPointer: State why the other two ratings fail — too low blows at switch-on, too high lets the surge through.

check.stem: A fuse protects an appliance by:

options.explanation: Fuses store nothing; they interrupt the circuit.

options.text: lowering the voltage at the socket
options.explanation: Fuses do not regulate voltage.

options.text: melting its wire and breaking the circuit when the current is too large
options.explanation: The melted wire opens the circuit and stops the excess flow.

options.text: cooling the wires with a heat sink
options.explanation: Cooling is not how a fuse acts.

check.stem: The standard household fuse ratings are:

options.explanation: Those are the three ratings met in domestic plugs.
Those are far below domestic plug ratings.
Those exceed the domestic plug standards.
A plausible-looking but incorrect set.

check.stem: An appliance needs 4 A from a 230 V mains. Its power is:

options.explanation: That divides the voltage by the current — the wrong way round.
Adding the two quantities is meaningless.
That doubles the correct answer for no reason.

check.stem: A fuse rated below the appliance's normal current will:

options.explanation: An underrating blows sooner, not later.

options.text: blow as soon as the appliance runs normally
options.explanation: The working current alone exceeds the rating, so it melts immediately.
The fuse cannot change the appliance's power.
The rating does not throttle the current before melting.

check.stem: The fuse chosen for an appliance should be:

options.explanation: An oversized fuse reacts far too late to protect anything.

options.text: exactly equal to the current it needs
options.explanation: A rating equal to the working current blows during normal running.

options.text: the next size up from the current it needs
options.explanation: One size up survives normal running yet still trips on a surge.
That would blow at once, like an underrating.

check.stem: State the equation used to find the current an appliance draws from its power and the mains voltage.
check.modelAnswer: I = P ÷ V — the current equals the power divided by the voltage.

check.stem: Why must the fuse rating sit above the appliance's normal current?
check.modelAnswer: A rating at or below the working current would melt during ordinary operation, so the fuse must sit just above it — the next standard size up.

check.stem: Explain why a 13 A fuse is a poor choice for a lamp that needs 0.2 A.
check.modelAnswer: The gap is enormous: the fuse would tolerate roughly thirteen amperes before melting, far beyond what the lamp survives, so a fault would wreck the lamp long before the fuse reacted.

check.stem: An appliance draws 3.1 A. Which standard fuse fits, and why?
check.modelAnswer: The 5 A fuse: a 3 A fuse would blow the moment the appliance switched on, while 13 A would allow ten extra amperes to flow before it blew — so the next size up, 5 A, is the correct choice.

glossary.definition: The rate of energy transfer — the energy a device moves per second, measured in watts.
The unit of power: one joule of energy transferred each second.
A safety device whose thin wire melts when the current is too large, breaking the circuit.
The current a fuse tolerates before melting; domestic plugs use 3 A, 5 A and 13 A.
A memory aid that reproduces the rearrangements of a three-term relationship.

workedExample.prompt: Calculate the potential difference across a 48 W electric motor carrying a current of 4 A.
steps: List the knowns: power P = 48 W and current I = 4 A.
State the linking equation: P = I × V.
Rearrange for voltage: V = P ÷ I.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The potential difference across the motor is 12 V.
